c.tagline: Cameroon's steamy economic hub and gateway to the coast.

taxi.fareNote: Shared yellow taxis charge a small fixed per-zone fare (rarely metered); private/whole-car hires and airport trips are negotiated upfront since meters aren't used.

emergency.medical: 119 (SAMU/medical emergency; 112 also routes to emergency services)
emergency.note: Response times can be slow and English may not be spoken by operators; hotels and private clinics (e.g. Polyclinique Bonanjo, Clinique de l'Aeroport) are often faster to contact directly for medical issues.

hood_landmark.Akwa: Hotel Akwa Palace, Boulevard de la Liberté, Douala
hood_landmark.Deido: Pont du Wouri (Wouri Bridge), Deido, Douala

avoid.reason: Petty/violent crime; caution at night. Note: Anglophone NW/SW and Far North regions have serious unrest — check advisories

hood_desc: Douala's historic colonial-era administrative quarter by the port, with embassies, ministries and old German trading houses; central and relatively secure by day, best for business travelers and history-minded visitors.

The buzzing commercial and nightlife heart of the city along Boulevard de la Liberté, packed with banks, shops, bars and restaurants; suits travelers who want to be in the thick of things and don't mind noise and traffic.
An upscale, leafy residential district favored by expats and diplomats with the city's best restaurants and boutique hotels; ideal for comfort-seekers wanting a calmer, greener base.
A traditional Sawa fishing neighborhood on the north bank of the Wouri River with lively local markets; suited to budget travelers wanting an authentic, less touristy experience.

A sprawling, fast-growing residential and business suburb popular with the Cameroonian middle class and long-stay visitors; good for those wanting modern serviced apartments away from downtown congestion, at the cost of a longer commute.
lodging: Foyer du Marin - Deutsche Seemannsmission Douala

water.note: Tap water is not safe to drink; use bottled water.

sys.n: Douala BRT (Bus Rapid Transit, under construction)

transit.pay: Most transport today is informal: passengers pay cash directly to shared-taxi drivers, minibus conductors, or moto-taxi (bendskin) riders for a fixed or negotiated per-zone fare. The planned BRT is expected to introduce a prepaid card/ticket system once operational.
transit.hours: Shared taxis and moto-taxis run roughly 6am-10pm; service thins out after dark, so visitors typically rely on ride-hailing apps or private/hotel cars at night.
transit.note: Douala has no metro, tram or formal city bus network yet; a Bus Rapid Transit line has been under construction since the mid-2020s. Yellow shared taxis and motorcycle taxis (bendskins, restricted in some central districts) currently fill the gap.

ferry: Small boats/canoes across the Wouri River to Bonabéri
Speedboat services to Limbe and Idenau

transit.m: No dedicated airport bus; shared minibus/clando from main road nearby (irregular, luggage-unfriendly)

tip.r: Tipping isn't obligatory; rounding up or leaving roughly 5-10% at restaurants and for hotel staff is appreciated but far from universal.
